sources.note: No descriptive (grammar/phonology/sketch) reference for Nyengo; only Johnston 1919 and Livingstone 1851 (both 'a wordlist or less') plus Fortune 1963 (overview/comparative, 'a wordlist or less', language note 'Nyengo = Nyengo [nye], Makoma = Nyengo [nye]'). Greater Luyana and Simaaic subgrouping rests on Lisimba 1982, whose abstract promises dialect comparison 'with respect to morphophonemics, lexicon, grammar and tone' but is not open.

sources.note: Nothing Nyengo-specific. n. 142: 'Next to Rotse is the Nyengo language, which is described in Livingstone's Comparative Vocabulary MSS. It is spoken on the River Nyengo, which is an affluent of the Upper Zambezi' (word examples only). His chapter 'On Accentuation in Bantu' (nn. 301-312) is pan-Bantu: 'That accent which consists in laying a light stress on the penult is generally less marked in Tonga than in Kafir.. The larger number of the Bantu languages seem to agree with Tonga in this respect'; Nyengo is not named there.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Nyengo is Johnston's language no. 82: 'NYENGO is apparently the speech of (amongst other tribes) the Ba-mpukushu. It is sometimes called South Luyi. Our vocabulary record of it is due to Livingstone's Banyenko vocabulary, which shows its affinities with Luyi, and in a much less degree with Yeye.' Only lexical/morphological remarks (goat -pongo, God -nyambe, negatives Ka- and -se-); no prosody.

sources.note: No Nyengo material (a full-text search for stress/accent over those folders: no hits). Related varieties only: Jacottet 1896 p.83 on Luyi K.31 'L'accent tonique retombe toujours sur la penultieme'; Yukawa 1987 treats Mwenyi as a two-tone language with no stress statement. Not transferable to Nyengo.

sources.citation: Bleek, Wilhelm H. I. 1862. A Comparative Grammar of South African Languages. Part I: Phonology. London: Truebner. (Glottolog ref 124005)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing Nyengo-specific. 'Banyenko' forms (from Livingstone's MS) appear only in the sound-correspondence and prefix tables. Sect. 375 is a Bantu-wide generalisation: 'In the Ba-ntu languages the accent lies, most generally, on the penultimate.. and it is shifted with a terminal increase of a word' (exceptions named: Kikamba, Otyiherero).
